Pasture Land: Pasture Land forms large open parcels separated by clear field boundaries or fences.
Pasture Land usually appears in green to yellow-brown tones across broad grassy areas.
Pasture Land has a fine, soft vegetation texture rather than the coarse canopy texture of Forest.
Pasture Land lacks the repeated row geometry that distinguishes Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land is more uniformly covered than Herbaceous Vegetation Land, with less natural patchiness inside each parcel.
Pasture Land often has irregular to moderately regular enclosure shapes rather than tightly gridded cultivated plots.
Pasture Land shows continuous grass cover without the strong bare-soil striping common in Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land is generally open, with very sparse buildings scattered far apart.
Pasture Land commonly lies beside narrow farm tracks or minor roads that trace parcel edges.
Pasture Land rarely contains dense tree clusters, leaving most of the field surface unobstructed.
Pasture Land presents smoother tonal variation across a parcel than mixed natural vegetation.
Pasture Land often appears as contiguous grazing blocks adjoining other agricultural fields.
Pasture Land has low vertical structure, so shadows from vegetation are minimal compared with Forest.
Pasture Land parcels are often broad and uninterrupted, not broken into many small orchard-like units.
Pasture Land may include small ponds or drainage lines, but water covers only a minor part of the parcel.
Pasture Land shows managed boundaries that are more legible than those in untended herbaceous cover.
Pasture Land tends to have consistent grass density across each enclosure instead of alternating planted bands.
Pasture Land usually lacks the checkerboard of contrasting crop stages seen in Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land is dominated by open vegetation surfaces with only occasional isolated trees along edges.
Pasture Land often creates a calm, even patch texture across fields, unlike the stronger linear patterns of cultivated classes.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land forms broad open patches with irregular natural boundaries rather than neat rectangular field blocks.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows a fine, even grassy texture without the dark coarse canopy pattern of forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land is dominated by light green to yellow-brown tones instead of the deeper shadowed greens of dense woody cover.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks visible plow lines or parallel row marks that are common in annual crop fields.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no orchard grid, vineyard striping, or evenly spaced planting points.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land usually appears as continuous low cover with only occasional scattered trees and no dominant crowns.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains little internal subdivision, unlike pasture that is often split into smaller enclosed paddocks.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has a soft natural surface pattern rather than the strongly segmented geometry of cultivated land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land often covers medium to large uninterrupted areas instead of many small managed parcels.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows sparse built structures, with no dense clusters of buildings or street grids.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has smooth-to-fine vegetation texture that is more uniform than mixed shrub or woodland mosaics.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land may be crossed by a few narrow tracks, but not by dense straight access networks.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land is generally dry land cover with no broad smooth water surfaces dominating the patch.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has edges that blend unevenly into nearby cover rather than sharp fence-like boundaries.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land presents open vegetation cover with very limited shadowing compared with taller forest stands.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks repeated alternating bands of cover that would suggest planted perennial rows.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land often appears as naturalistic expanses between other land covers rather than as engineered lots.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land maintains a fairly consistent low vegetation density across the patch without bare-soil striping.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land is less rectilinear and less regularly enclosed than managed pasture landscapes.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows broad grassy cover uninterrupted by major canals, reservoirs, or dense road infrastructure.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road appears as a long narrow corridor that crosses the scene with continuous linear connectivity.
Highway or Road has fairly uniform width over long distances, unlike rivers that widen, narrow, and meander.
Highway or Road shows straight segments and sharp angles created by engineered construction.
Highway or Road often forms branching junctions and intersections rather than isolated compact patches.
Highway or Road is usually gray, white, or very dark compared with surrounding vegetation or bare ground.
Highway or Road has a smooth homogeneous surface texture with little internal variation.
Highway or Road contrasts with residential buildings by remaining a thin linear feature instead of a dense cluster of small rectangles.
Highway or Road contrasts with industrial buildings by lacking large blocky roofs and area-filling compounds.
Highway or Road commonly follows parallel edges that create a clear corridor shape.
Highway or Road may be bordered by thin roadside strips, but the central feature stays narrower than adjacent land parcels.
Highway or Road cuts through herbaceous vegetation as a crisp high-contrast line rather than a broad textured field.
Highway or Road tends to connect multiple built-up areas, creating a network pattern across the landscape.
Highway or Road keeps regular boundaries with clean edges rather than the irregular banks of water channels.
Highway or Road can appear as paired parallel lanes separated by a narrow median.
Highway or Road occupies a small fraction of area relative to its length, emphasizing its elongated form.
Highway or Road often aligns with urban blocks and other planned infrastructure in an organized layout.
Highway or Road remains mostly non-vegetated, with adjacent greenery appearing only as edge cover or nearby parcels.
Highway or Road crosses the scene as a continuous band, while building classes break into many discrete footprints.
Highway or Road may include overpasses or interchanges that create curved connectors attached to the main linear route.
Highway or Road rarely contains visible water tones within the corridor, helping separate it from rivers and canals.
Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land shows a mosaic of rectangular and polygonal fields separated by sharp visible boundaries.
Annual Crop Land often contains neighboring parcels with contrasting tan, brown, and green tones within the same agricultural block.
Annual Crop Land has strong human-made geometric regularity, with field edges forming straight lines and clean angles.
Annual Crop Land commonly includes bare or lightly vegetated plots mixed beside greener parcels, unlike the more uniformly grassy cover of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land displays fine, even texture inside each field, with abrupt texture changes from one parcel to the next.
Annual Crop Land lacks the repeated dot or row-crown pattern that marks Permanent Crop Land orchards and groves.
Annual Crop Land usually has low vegetation cover that does not create the dense dark canopy typical of Forest.
Annual Crop Land is frequently crossed by narrow farm tracks or dirt roads running parallel to parcel edges.
Annual Crop Land may show drainage or irrigation lines as thin linear features aligned with the field layout.
Annual Crop Land tends to form medium to large parcels that fit together as an organized patchwork rather than irregular natural vegetation patches.
Annual Crop Land often includes recently worked soil surfaces that appear smooth and exposed compared with Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land has sharply bounded cultivated units, unlike the broader and softer-edged expanses typical of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land can show alternating light and dark strips caused by different field surface conditions within adjacent plots.
Annual Crop Land usually presents a managed open landscape with very sparse tree cover inside the parcel interiors.
Annual Crop Land may contain occasional straight canals or ditches marking field divisions and water control routes.
Annual Crop Land often has access roads touching multiple parcel corners and edges in a deliberate gridlike arrangement.
Annual Crop Land shows vegetation that is short and spatially ordered, without the continuous irregular texture of natural herbaceous cover.
Annual Crop Land can include some fields with muted brown or gray soil tones beside others with bright green growth stages.
Annual Crop Land generally has parcel shapes more regular and angular than the rounded or uneven patches of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land sometimes includes small water channels or ponds embedded within a strictly organized field pattern.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings consists of many small to medium rectangular roofs packed closely together within a compact urban patch.
Residential Buildings is organized by short local streets and frequent intersections rather than by a few broad transport corridors.
Residential Buildings often forms neighborhood blocks and cul-de-sacs with repeated curving or gridlike street layouts.
Residential Buildings shows a fine-grained mix of roofs, driveways, and small yards instead of the large continuous structures of Industrial Buildings.
Residential Buildings has moderate tree cover scattered between houses, creating a speckled green-and-gray texture.
Residential Buildings usually contains less extensive open paving than Industrial Buildings, with impervious surfaces broken up by parcels.
Residential Buildings presents regular parcelized patterns with sharp property divisions rather than irregular natural textures.
Residential Buildings commonly appears in medium-density clusters where individual buildings remain distinct but tightly spaced.
Residential Buildings has roof colors dominated by gray, brown, white, or dark tones interspersed with small green patches.
Residential Buildings is crossed by narrow branching roads that serve homes rather than long straight highways dominating the scene.
Residential Buildings lacks the long parallel planting rows that characterize Annual Crop Land and Permanent Crop Land.
Residential Buildings forms a mosaic of built lots and vegetation that is much finer in texture than uniform agricultural parcels.
Residential Buildings often has clear block edges where neighborhood development contrasts sharply with adjacent open land or vegetation.
Residential Buildings contains repeated small building footprints aligned along streets instead of a few oversized warehouse-like rectangles.
Residential Buildings may include small retention ponds or channels, but water is usually secondary to the dense roof-and-street pattern.
Residential Buildings shows short setbacks and small open spaces around structures rather than broad empty yards or loading areas.
Residential Buildings frequently combines straight street segments with curved residential loops, producing an intricate suburban pattern.
Residential Buildings has a balanced mix of impervious surfaces and vegetation, unlike roads-only patches where pavement dominates nearly all of the area.
Residential Buildings tends to have internal street networks with many dead ends and side streets instead of simple elongated linear strips.
Residential Buildings appears as contiguous neighborhood fabric with repeated house lots, not as isolated buildings surrounded by large fields.
Forest: Forest shows large contiguous patches of dense tree cover rather than many small agricultural parcels.
Forest has dark green to deep green tones across most of the area.
Forest displays a coarse, mottled texture created by individual tree crowns and canopy shadows.
Forest lacks the smooth, even surface typical of Herbaceous Vegetation Land or Pasture Land.
Forest usually has irregular outer boundaries that follow terrain instead of straight field edges.
Forest contains few visible internal divisions compared with Annual Crop Land or Pasture Land.
Forest does not show the repeated parallel rows typical of Permanent Crop Land.
Forest has a closed canopy appearance with very little bare soil visible between vegetation.
Forest often includes shadowed pockets within the canopy that make the surface darker and more varied.
Forest is dominated by natural vegetation patterns rather than gridlike street layouts or blocky development.
Forest may be crossed by only a few narrow roads or tracks, with built structures scarce or absent.
Forest tends to form broad wooded masses instead of the narrow strips common in some managed fields.
Forest has less color variation from parcel to parcel than cropland mosaics with mixed growth stages.
Forest commonly follows ridges, slopes, or drainage lines rather than a rigid rectangular layout.
Forest shows rounded and uneven patch shapes rather than crisp geometric planting blocks.
Forest has a vertically structured canopy texture that appears rougher than grass-covered land.
Forest rarely contains the regular spacing of trees seen in orchards or plantation-style crop rows.
Forest presents continuous woody cover with only occasional small clearings interrupting the canopy.
Forest can border rivers or streams with dense dark vegetation extending right to the water edge.
Forest has very low roof and pavement presence compared with developed or mixed rural settlement areas.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land consists of medium to large parcels with sharp boundaries and a clear geometric layout.
Permanent Crop Land shows evenly spaced tree or vine rows forming repeated linear patterns across each field.
Permanent Crop Land often has dot-like or grid-like canopy spacing that separates individual plants unlike the smoother cover of pasture.
Permanent Crop Land contains alternating bands of vegetation and exposed soil or short ground cover between planted lines.
Permanent Crop Land has a structured texture that repeats in one consistent row direction across an entire parcel.
Permanent Crop Land displays woody vegetation in organized lines rather than the dense continuous canopy typical of forest.
Permanent Crop Land often appears as elongated or rectangular plots with internal planting alignment matching the field edges.
Permanent Crop Land shows parcel-scale regularity where tonal changes follow field boundaries instead of irregular natural patches.
Permanent Crop Land commonly includes narrow farm tracks or straight access lanes dividing blocks of planted rows.
Permanent Crop Land has a more discrete and patterned canopy texture than annual cropland with uniform continuous cover.
Permanent Crop Land may show terraced bands of perennial planting on slopes with repeated contour-parallel lines.
Permanent Crop Land often mixes dark green plant rows with lighter brown or pale green inter-row strips.
Permanent Crop Land contains repeated clumps or small crowns at regular intervals, creating a planted orchard texture.
Permanent Crop Land usually has lower canopy closure than forest because gaps between planted rows remain visible.
Permanent Crop Land can form large contiguous blocks where every parcel shares a deliberate row spacing and planting rhythm.
Permanent Crop Land often has straighter parcel edges and more persistent internal alignment than herbaceous vegetation land.
Permanent Crop Land may include scattered small agricultural buildings placed along field edges rather than dense settlement clusters.
Permanent Crop Land sometimes borders irrigation ponds or channels, but the planted row geometry remains the dominant pattern.
Permanent Crop Land shows vegetation density organized by rows and columns rather than the diffuse spread of pasture grass.
Permanent Crop Land frequently presents a checker of separate orchard or vineyard blocks, each with its own consistent row orientation.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings show very large rectangular roof blocks that occupy much bigger footprints than the small units of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings often form clusters of long warehouse or factory halls arranged on broad parcels with clear spacing between structures.
Industrial Buildings are dominated by gray, white, or dark impervious surfaces with far less green cover than crop land or residential blocks.
Industrial Buildings include wide paved yards surrounding the buildings, creating large open hard-surfaced areas absent from most Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings have sharp rectilinear outlines and highly regular block geometry rather than the organic texture of vegetation.
Industrial Buildings are commonly linked by wide access roads and internal service lanes, but the scene is dominated by building masses rather than a single linear corridor like Highway or Road.
Industrial Buildings show sparse, fragmented vegetation confined to edges or medians instead of the continuous planted texture of Annual Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings lack the repetitive row or orchard grid patterns that distinguish Permanent Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings usually contain a few very large structures per parcel rather than many tightly packed small rooftops.
Industrial Buildings often include expansive parking or loading surfaces adjacent to roofs, producing broad uniform paved patches.
Industrial Buildings have a coarse blocky texture created by large roofs and open pavement, unlike the fine-grained pattern of dense housing.
Industrial Buildings frequently appear in organized complexes with parallel or orthogonal building alignment across the site.
Industrial Buildings tend to have straight property edges and rectangular compounds with little irregular natural boundary shape.
Industrial Buildings often present strong contrast between bright roofs and darker asphalt yards within the same complex.
Industrial Buildings are typically embedded in built-up zones with connected street grids, not isolated among continuous agricultural fields.
Industrial Buildings show larger setbacks and wider spacing between structures than Residential Buildings, leaving visible open paved ground.
Industrial Buildings may include open storage pads or bare hardstand areas that read as plain geometric surfaces beside the roofs.
Industrial Buildings usually have minimal tree canopy, with vegetation appearing as scattered strips rather than dense patches.
Industrial Buildings rarely contain water features, and the visible surface is overwhelmingly roof and pavement.
Industrial Buildings stand out from Annual Crop Land by lacking soil-tone field mosaics and instead showing contiguous industrial parcels with massive rectangular buildings.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake forms a broad contiguous water area that covers much more width than a river channel.
Sea or Lake has a smooth interior surface with little visible texture compared with grassy or pasture land.
Sea or Lake is usually dark blue, blue-green, or gray across a large continuous patch.
Sea or Lake lacks the rectangular field boundaries that break up herbaceous vegetation and pasture areas.
Sea or Lake shows no street grid or dense building footprints within the main water surface.
Sea or Lake is enclosed or bordered by a distinct shoreline that sharply separates open water from land.
Sea or Lake often has a rounded, lobed, or irregular basin shape rather than a thin meandering line.
Sea or Lake contains wide open water uninterrupted by frequent banks, bars, or crossings seen in rivers.
Sea or Lake may include bright sun-glint patches sitting on an otherwise uniform dark surface.
Sea or Lake occupies a compact or expansive basin-like patch instead of a narrow elongated corridor.
Sea or Lake has interior tones that remain fairly even without the mottled plant texture of vegetated land.
Sea or Lake commonly shows coves or inlets cut into the shoreline around a large open-water body.
Sea or Lake presents a clear land-water boundary with adjacent vegetation or soil stopping abruptly at the edge.
Sea or Lake does not display parallel plow lines, pasture tracks, or other agricultural striping patterns.
Sea or Lake appears as one dominant water mass rather than multiple small segmented patches.
Sea or Lake may border developed land, but the water area itself remains free of road networks and blocks.
Sea or Lake has a shoreline that wraps around a wide basin, unlike rivers whose banks stay close together.
Sea or Lake often spans enough area that opposite shores are separated by a large uniform water interior.
Sea or Lake lacks the dense tufted or patchy texture typical of herbaceous vegetation land.
Sea or Lake shows an open expanse whose width stays substantial over long stretches, distinguishing it from rivers.
River: River forms a long narrow water corridor that crosses the scene instead of a broad enclosed water body.
River usually follows a sinuous path with repeated bends rather than the straighter alignment of a road or canal.
River often shows branching tributary connections that join into a connected drainage pattern.
River has irregular natural banks instead of the crisp parallel edges typical of highways or paved roads.
River is commonly dark blue, dark green, or gray, with a smooth surface contrasting with textured land.
River varies gradually in width along its course rather than keeping a uniform engineered width.
River creates a continuous elongated shape rather than many small scattered dark patches.
River is often bordered by thin ribbons of vegetation that trace both sides of the channel.
River separates adjacent land covers with sharp tonal boundaries between smooth water and rougher fields or forest.
River may contain small point bars or sediment-toned inner bends that follow channel curvature.
River occupies low winding corridors through the landscape rather than filling a wide rounded basin like a lake.
River can meander across floodplain areas, producing looping curves and occasional oxbow-like side shapes.
River lacks lane markings, median strips, and the consistently straight segments associated with transport routes.
River may appear braided in places, with multiple narrow water threads separated by light sediment bars.
River commonly narrows upstream and widens downstream, producing directional change in channel scale.
River cuts through vegetated terrain as a dark linear opening, unlike forest which remains densely textured throughout.
River edges are uneven and naturally scalloped rather than rectangular or grid-aligned.
River often links multiple bends into one connected course that extends beyond the frame.
River shows smoother interior texture than surrounding canopy, crops, or built surfaces.
River follows a branching inland channel pattern rather than the broad open expanse of sea water.
